dailyBrief.text: Good morning — Solon gets a sunny, dry day today with a high near 72° after a clear 48° start, and Thursday warms further to about 76°. Overnight, the World Series refused to end: Tampa Bay scored twice in the 12th to walk off Milwaukee 4-3 and stave off a sweep, though the Brewers still lead 3-1 with Game 5 tonight at 8:08 PM. In Israel, the actual vote count kept both blocs short of a majority, with Netanyahu and Eisenkot staking rival claims, and at home the FEC's filing system was hit by hackers a week before the midterms. Tonight in Cleveland, the Cavs host Washington at Rocket Arena at 7 PM, and early in-person voting runs 7:30 AM to 7:30 PM today — with mailed ballots now needing to be received, not just postmarked, by 7:30 PM on Nov. 3.

weekBrief.text: The rest of the week in Solon is a temperature roller coaster: sunny and 72° today, up to about 76° Thursday with a shower chance late Thursday night, then a sharp cool-down to 59° Friday before a dry, mild, mostly cloudy Halloween at 61° and a warmer 68° Sunday — when clocks fall back an hour. It is a huge sports stretch: World Series Game 5 tonight with Milwaukee up 3-1, the Cavs hosting Washington tonight and playing at Atlanta Thursday and Milwaukee on Halloween, Ohio State at USC Saturday night with freshman Luke Fahey expected to make his first start, and the 5-2 Browns at 5-2 Pittsburgh on Sunday for first place. It is also the final week of Ohio early voting — in-person hours run through Sunday Nov. 1 ahead of Election Day Nov. 3, and the Brown-Husted Senate race is deadlocked at 47-44. The standout deal is Giant Eagle's $0.99 avocados, but that ad ends today. And with the baby due in early November, this is car-seat-check and finishing-touches week at home.

Netanyahu and Eisenkot stake rival claims as Israel's vote count leaves both blocs short of a majority
items.summary:
Israel's election moved from exit polls to an actual count overnight, and the picture stayed deadlocked. With about two-thirds of votes counted on Wednesday morning, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition was tracking around 54 seats against roughly 48 for the opposition, and updated exit polls put the two blocs anywhere from tied at 51-51 to a narrow 52-49 edge for Netanyahu — none of it close to the 61 seats needed to govern the 120-seat Knesset.

Both leaders spoke in the small hours. Netanyahu, 77, called for a strong right-wing national government and pointed to military successes, while former military chief Gadi Eisenkot said voters had rejected Netanyahu and urged him to retire, warning him not to use security for political purposes. Turnout hit 77.7%, the highest in more than two decades, and Arab parties were on course for around 18 seats — nearly double their 2022 haul — after a historic surge in turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel.

The stalemate matters because Eisenkot has all but ruled out governing with the Arab parties, which narrows his own path, while Netanyahu's bloc leans on far-right religious parties projected at about 13 seats. Israel could be headed for weeks of coalition bargaining with Netanyahu staying on as caretaker, or even another election.

Final results are expected Thursday or Friday, once roughly 600,000-plus double-envelope ballots from soldiers, diplomats and hospital patients are counted, with official publication due Nov. 4.

items.title: Zelenskiy says Ukraine is retaking ground in pipeline and other offensives, in its strongest position in some time
items.summary:
President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said Tuesday night that Ukrainian forces are retaking territory through a series of offensives, and he revealed for the first time an operation called Veles near Kupiansk in the northeastern Kharkiv region. In it, Ukrainian troops used underground gas pipelines to outflank Russian positions — turning against Moscow a tactic Russia had previously tried on them. Zelenskiy called Veles a strong, well-planned, technology-driven operation with extraordinary success.

He also pointed to an air assault operation in eastern Ukraine and a second effort, Vivaldi, further north, meant to block Russian advances toward Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, the so-called fortress-belt cities. A senior commander reported last month that Ukraine's Third Army Corps had cleared 75 square kilometers of Russian infiltration groups and recaptured another 10 square kilometers in that sector. Zelenskiy added that an August offensive further south returned 26 villages to Ukrainian control.

Kyiv's claim is that its battlefield position is the strongest it has been in some time in the four-and-a-half-year war, and could improve further with more Western air-defense deliveries. Russia tells a different story: its top general said this month Moscow had captured 92 settlements since early September, claims Ukraine's military dismisses, and the Kremlin continues to insist on an overall settlement that includes all of Donbas.

What to watch is whether the newly claimed gains hold over the coming weeks, and whether fresh air-defense systems actually arrive from Western allies.

items.title: Norway's prime minister defends a rare call with Putin as making sure Europe's views are heard
items.summary:
Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Stoere on Wednesday defended a rare three-way call with Vladimir Putin and Finland's president, saying the point was to make sure the Russian leader hears European views directly, not only American ones. The 90-minute call on Tuesday broke a long-standing Western European practice of shunning direct contact with the Kremlin.

Stoere told broadcaster NRK he does not expect Putin to change his mind, but worried that some European messages do not reach him when only the Americans talk to him. Norway used the call to push de-escalation steps: stopping attacks on energy infrastructure in both countries, halting strikes on ships exporting Ukrainian grain, and more prisoner-of-war exchanges. The leaders spoke to Zelenskiy afterward, and Finland's Alexander Stubb called the discussion frank and substantive.

Not everyone applauded. Denmark's prime minister criticized the outreach, Sweden's leader saw little hope of a breakthrough, and the Kremlin's own readout suggested no softening — Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said the call offered nothing new and that Europeans were simply seeking a role in negotiations. The call comes ahead of expected face-to-face talks between Ukrainian and Russian officials in Abu Dhabi next month, with U.S. officials also involved.

The stakes are about who shapes any settlement. Stoere noted Russia controls nearly 20% of Ukraine, that Kyiv will never sign away territory, and that the hardest question is what security guarantees Ukraine gets afterward.

items.title: A local truce around Oleshky in southern Ukraine lets aid reach trapped civilians
items.summary:
Russia and Ukraine have halted fighting in designated areas around Oleshky, a town on the Russian-held left bank of the Dnipro in Ukraine's Kherson region, so aid can reach the civilians still trapped there. The ceasefire took effect at 3 a.m. Kyiv time on Oct. 27, has since been extended across the region, and both sides say no breaches have been reported. Ukrainian politician Davyd Arakhamia said it is due to run until Nov. 1.

Oleshky had about 24,000 residents before the invasion; roughly 1,700 to 2,000 remain, mostly elderly, including about 50 children. The situation is described as critical: drones carrying food no longer reach the town, roads are mined, and constant Russian drone activity makes it hard to leave. The plan is to deliver food, medicine and drinking water, then have civilian representatives from both countries assess needs and prepare evacuations for those who want out.

The White House announced the pause on Oct. 23 and says it came through an initiative of First Lady Melania Trump; the start was brought forward two days and the area widened so convoys could pass safely. Ukrainian authorities have asked people not to publish convoy routes or timings.

This is a narrow humanitarian window, not a wider ceasefire — fighting has continued elsewhere in Ukraine even as the convoys move.

items.title: EU leaders clash over 'associate membership' for Canada ahead of the Montreal summit
items.summary:
The European Union and Canada hold their 21st summit in Montreal on Thursday and Friday, and on substance everyone agrees: ties should deepen. European Council President António Costa, Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney are set to launch an 'Alliance for the Future' covering trade, digital policy, critical raw materials, defence, security, research and youth, nine months after Carney's praised Davos warning that middle powers must act together.

The fight is over a label. In her September State of the Union speech, von der Leyen proposed making Canada an 'associate member' of the EU — a status that does not actually exist — without consulting member states first. Paris and Berlin were displeased, and Germany was further irritated because Chancellor Friedrich Merz had floated a similar associate idea in May for Ukraine's path to membership. EU ambassadors failed to agree on wording Monday, and a fallback silence procedure failed Tuesday.

Carney, for his part, says he does not intend to join the EU and prefers 'unique alliance' language, along with progress ratifying the CETA trade deal — provisionally in force since 2017, trade up more than 80% over a decade, but still not ratified by nine member states including France and Italy. At home, a late-September poll found 70% of Canadians liked the associate-status idea, while Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre calls it a loss of sovereignty.

What to watch: whether ambassadors settle the wording on Wednesday, a day before the summit opens, and what concrete initiatives the alliance actually contains once the terminology fight ends.

items.title: China dismisses Taiwan's accusations over a plot to attack a comedian who mocked Xi
items.summary:
China on Wednesday dismissed Taiwan's accusations that Beijing was behind a plot to attack a Taiwanese comedian whose shows mocked President Xi Jinping, calling the case a fabrication by Taiwan's ruling party. Taiwanese prosecutors have indicted five people over the alleged plot against comedian Huang Yi-hao.

According to prosecutors, the defendants were paid to fake a car accident and 'break the arms and legs' of Huang so he could not perform; in the end he was only lightly injured in last month's attack. Taiwan's government frames the case as 'transnational repression' against people Beijing views as separatists or politically suspect, and Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung told lawmakers Wednesday it showed China's expanding efforts to challenge personal safety and freedom of expression.

Beijing's Taiwan Affairs Office spokesperson Chen Binhua told a regular news conference the narrative is trotted out every time there is an election on the island — a reference to Taiwan's local elections next month — and called it a tired routine meant to stir anti-China sentiment and promote independence.

The exchange is the latest in a running dispute: Taiwan points to other attacks on China critics, including Hong Kong singer and activist Denise Ho in Taipei in 2019, while Beijing insists Taiwan is part of China and that only Taiwanese people — a formulation Taipei rejects — will decide the island's future.

items.title: Trump says he will respect the midterm results 'if they're honest elections'
items.summary:
President Donald Trump told reporters on Tuesday that he will respect the Nov. 3 midterm results only if the elections are 'honest.' Asked directly at Joint Base Andrews as he left for a campaign trip to Texas, he said: 'I will if they're honest elections.'

The comment lands with polling pointing to a possible blue wave: Democrats are widely favoured to win the House and have several viable paths to the Senate. Asked how he would work with Democrats if Republicans lost both chambers, Trump said he would use his veto pen often and find ways to make deals, noting it has happened to presidents before.

The remark sits alongside other steps that have raised the temperature around the vote. The Justice Department last week sued to block Alaska's certification of its Senate race if Republicans lose, Trump announced a $1 million payment for voter-fraud tips that lead to an arrest or conviction, and he has directed Homeland Security to look for noncitizens on state voting rolls while not ruling out a national emergency around the midterms. Trump has regularly accused Democrats of cheating without presenting evidence.

Why it matters: conditioning acceptance of the results a week before Election Day sets up a contested aftermath if the night goes against Republicans, in a country where his refusal to accept the 2020 result culminated in the Jan. 6, 2021 Capitol attack.

items.title: New Marist poll: 44% say their midterm vote is a vote against Trump, and Democrats lead the generic ballot by 8
items.summary:
A Marist poll conducted for NPR and PBS News and released Tuesday found that 44% of likely voters describe their November vote as a vote against President Trump, compared with 21% who say they are voting to support him. Among independents, voters were more than three times as likely to say they are voting against Trump as to support him.

The same poll gave Democrats an 8-point lead over Republicans on the generic congressional ballot. The top issue for voters was the cost of living at 34%, narrowly ahead of preserving democracy at 33%, with immigration at 12% and foreign policy and health care at 5% each. On personal finances, 38% said theirs had gotten worse over the past year and 44% said they had stayed about the same.

The survey of 1,289 registered voters was conducted Oct. 19-20 with a margin of error of 3.8 points. It fits the broader approval backdrop: polling averages in late October put Trump's approval around 37-38% against roughly 60% disapproval.

With less than a week to Election Day, the numbers suggest the midterms are functioning as a referendum on the president — the pattern that usually drives the out-party's turnout advantage — and that economic frustration, more than any single policy fight, is what GOP candidates have to overcome down-ballot.

items.title: Hackers target the FEC's filing system a week before the midterms, blinding campaign-finance disclosure
items.summary:
The Federal Election Commission's electronic filing system has been disrupted by a hacking attempt a week before the Nov. 3 elections, according to an internal email seen by Reuters. 'We have a bad actor attempting to breach FEC systems,' an FEC electronic filings officer wrote. 'As a result, we've had to temporarily shut down our web facing services.'

The filing system had been down since about 10 p.m. ET Monday. Previously filed reports remained searchable, and by Tuesday evening a status message said the problem had been identified and a fix was being implemented, though the system was still offline. A person familiar with the response described the attempt as narrow and compartmentalized, with cybersecurity staff shutting down the targeted parts; no attribution has been established, and it may have involved advanced AI models with hacking capabilities.

The FEC does not run elections, so ballots themselves are unaffected. What is blocked is disclosure: campaigns and groups cannot file the 24-hour and 48-hour reports that reveal last-minute spending on specific races. OpenSecrets' research director called it a big deal, noting super PACs and dark-money groups averaged over $50 million a day in the past week, with more than $250 million reported on Oct. 20 alone.

The timing is the story. AdImpact puts 2026 midterm ad spending and reservations at roughly $11.21 billion — already the most expensive U.S. election ever — and the disclosure blackout covers exactly the final-days money rush voters would most want to see.

items.title: Four Senate Democrats set a high bar for the permitting bill: restore the cancelled clean-energy grants first
items.summary:
Four Senate Democrats — Tammy Duckworth, Ron Wyden, Ed Markey and Jeff Merkley — pressed the Trump administration on Tuesday to begin restoring billions of dollars in cancelled clean-energy grants before a key vote on the bipartisan permitting bill, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026.

The bill, introduced Sept. 30 by Republican Shelley Moore Capito with Mike Lee, Sheldon Whitehouse and Martin Heinrich, would speed federal approval of energy and infrastructure projects, set deadlines for environmental reviews, limit some legal challenges, and accelerate power plants, transmission and grid modernisation. A procedural vote to advance it is expected Nov. 9, in the lame-duck session after the midterms.

In a letter to the bill's authors, the four senators asked the Energy Department to start reinstating grants terminated in October 2025 — about $8 billion worth — with a clear timeline, let recipients draw funds on the original terms, and pledge in writing not to cancel grants based on a state's politics. They pointed to a court filing in which the department acknowledged politics played a role in choosing which grants to kill. The letter stops short of an ultimatum but calls restoration 'compelling,' and warns the bill could hand Trump new tools to favour fossil fuels.

The fight shows the bill's obstacle is trust, not text: even its Democratic co-authors want more stalled renewables projects approved, while some House Democrats say it threatens community input and could supercharge the data-centre buildout.

items.title: Senate control could hang in limbo for weeks after Election Day
items.summary:
Do not expect to know who controls the Senate on election night — or maybe for weeks after. Axios reports that a slew of tight races and state-specific counting rules could leave Senate leaders guessing well into November about which party holds the chamber.

The scenarios branch sharply. A Republican majority would ease pressure on Majority Leader John Thune to move quickly on nominations. A Democratic majority would hand Minority Leader Chuck Schumer real leverage in the lame-duck session. And a 50-50 split would force the two parties to start negotiating a power-sharing agreement before anyone can organize the chamber.

Forecasters see a genuinely open race: Decision Desk HQ's late-October model gave Democrats about a 57% chance of winning the Senate (projected 51 seats) and a 79% chance of winning the House, with a Democratic sweep of both chambers the single most likely outcome. The Cook Political Report rates seven Senate seats as pure toss-ups — Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Ohio and Texas — six of them currently held by Republicans. All 435 House seats and 35 Senate seats are on the Nov. 3 ballot.

What to watch: slow-counting states, recounts, and certification fights like the Justice Department's Alaska lawsuit could keep control — and with it nominations and lame-duck legislation — unresolved well past Election Day.

items.title: SK Hynix profit jumps more than sevenfold to a record, with a $75 billion shareholder-return plan
items.summary:
South Korean memory-chip maker SK Hynix reported third-quarter operating profit of 83.3 trillion won — more than seven times the 11.4 trillion won of a year earlier and a record high — beating the LSEG SmartEstimate of 76.7 trillion won. Revenue rose 328% to 104.6 trillion won as AI-infrastructure demand pushed memory prices sharply higher.

SK Hynix, a key supplier to Nvidia, also announced shareholder returns totalling about 100 trillion won (roughly $75 billion) for 2026, split between cash dividends and share repurchases and cancellations. U.S.-listed SK Hynix shares jumped about 7.8% in premarket trading Wednesday, rival Micron gained around 4%, and Western Digital rose about 4.5%, while Seagate fell after its own results.

The print matters because Nvidia's memory suppliers had faced investor pressure to return more cash after shares slid from June record highs on doubts about how durable U.S. AI spending really is. A sevenfold profit jump is the first hard evidence this earnings week that the AI boom is still converting into cash, not just orders.

What to watch: Samsung reports next, and Microsoft and Alphabet report Wednesday night — together they will set the tone for whether the AI trade's October wobble is over.

items.title: Banks and Blackstone line up $63 billion to finance Broadcom AI chips for Anthropic
items.summary:
Bank of America, Citi, Morgan Stanley and Blackstone will provide $63 billion in financing to buy Broadcom AI chips and networking gear for Anthropic — one of the largest debt deals yet tied to the AI buildout, and the financing follow-up to Anthropic's IPO filing announced Monday.

The structure is elaborate. A newly formed special-purpose vehicle will purchase Broadcom XPU accelerators and networking equipment and lease them to Anthropic, the maker of Claude. About $43.5 billion — roughly 69% — is first-lien senior debt arranged by the three banks; Blackstone is the sole provider of the junior, second-lien money. Unusually, Broadcom itself is providing 'residual value support' equal to the first-lien portion, effectively guaranteeing lenders against the equipment losing value or Anthropic defaulting. Deliveries are expected to begin in 2027.

Broadcom CEO Hock Tan spent nearly two months lining the banks up; some lenders wavered on price and risk before higher rates were agreed in last-minute weekend talks. Broadcom shares climbed about 4% Tuesday on the deal, helping lift the Nasdaq.

The stakes: AI infrastructure is increasingly funded with structured debt and chipmaker guarantees rather than cash on balance sheets — a shift that spreads the risk of the buildout across Wall Street, and concentrates it if AI demand ever disappoints.

items.title: OpenAI plans to buy Google's AI chips outright, The Information reports
items.summary:
OpenAI plans to buy Google's AI chips, The Information reported Tuesday, citing a person familiar with the matter. No financial terms, volumes, chip generation or timing were disclosed; Google did not immediately comment and OpenAI declined to comment.

The move would deepen an already tangled relationship. The two companies compete head-on in AI products and search, yet keep doing business: last week OpenAI said it would make its frontier models available through Google Cloud. OpenAI is one of the largest buyers of Nvidia GPUs, and Reuters reported in June 2025 that it had begun renting Google's Tensor Processing Units — buying them outright would be a step further. OpenAI is also hiring engineers to optimize its models for TPUs, a sign of real engineering commitment, though the work is described as early-stage.

Google is pushing TPUs as a cheaper alternative to Nvidia and began selling them directly to some customers this year; on Tuesday it also announced Oracle will be the first major cloud outside Google to offer TPUs. Alphabet shares rose about 1.2% in premarket trading Wednesday on the report.

Why it matters: a direct purchase by Nvidia's marquee customer would loosen Nvidia's grip on AI hardware and give Alphabet a second AI revenue engine. Alphabet reports earnings Wednesday night, with most TPU revenue expected to be recognized in 2027.

items.title: Boeing shares plunge about 11% after a 737 ramp delay pushes its cash-flow recovery out a year
items.summary:
Boeing stock closed Tuesday down 10.69% at $168.18, touching a 52-week low on volume nearly six times its three-month average, after the planemaker pushed its 737 production ramp out by about a year. Management now expects to stabilize at 47 jets a month only early next year, with the 52-a-month target pushed to the second half of 2027, and Boeing will miss its goal of 500 737 MAX deliveries this year.

The quarter itself was mixed. Boeing delivered 161 jets, one more than a year ago; commercial revenue grew just 1% with a loss of about $700 million, while defense sales rose 15% to a $492 million profit and services grew 4% with $1 billion in operating profit. Reported revenue was about $24.2 billion with an adjusted loss of $0.34 a share, worse than the roughly $0.20-0.25 loss analysts expected. The backlog still grew 17.3% to $745.4 billion.

The real damage was in the guidance: free cash flow of about $2 billion in 2026, $3 billion in 2027 and $6 billion in 2028, reaching the $10 billion annual target in 2029 instead of 2028 — well below the $5.6 billion analysts had pencilled in for 2027. Morningstar cut its fair-value estimate to $242 from $254. Offsetting wins: the FAA certified the 737-7 in the quarter and the larger 737-10 in October, and the 777X remains on track for first delivery in 2027.

About half of Boeing's enterprise value rides on the 737 line, so the ramp pace is the single biggest driver of its long turnaround — and that driver just slipped another year.

items.title: Visa beats estimates as payments volume rises 9% to $4.08 trillion
items.summary:
Visa reported fiscal fourth-quarter results after the close Tuesday that beat Wall Street estimates, with adjusted earnings of $3.48 a share against the $3.44 average analyst forecast. Payments volume rose 9% to $4.08 trillion, up from $3.73 trillion a year earlier and slightly ahead of expectations.

Visa's numbers are watched as a window into consumer health worldwide, and this quarter's read is resilience: spending held up despite geopolitical uncertainty, higher interest rates and fuel-price pressure from Middle East conflicts. September's retail sales gain of 0.77% month over month, cited in Fed-day coverage, points the same way. 'Whenever technology changes commerce, we move with it,' CEO Ryan McInerney said, calling Visa the leading hyperscaler of payments globally.

The company is also expanding its perimeter. In August it agreed to buy fraud-prevention firm BioCatch for $2.4 billion in cash, and earlier in October it won approval from the People's Bank of China to begin preparations for a domestic bank-card clearing business in China.

What to watch: cross-border volume in the full release — the most economically sensitive line in Visa's results, and the one that would crack first if the consumer finally blinks.

items.title: AI stocks lift Wall Street Tuesday; the Fed is expected to hold Wednesday while Microsoft and Alphabet report
items.summary:
Wall Street climbed Tuesday on AI stocks: the Nasdaq Composite rose 1.18% to 26,477.81, the S&P 500 gained 0.60% to 7,722.60, and the Dow inched up 0.03% to 52,377.57. Technology shares rose 1.7% while energy fell 2.1%, and the VIX fear gauge dropped to 17.52 as sentiment recovered from a bruising first half of October.

Two forces did the lifting: Anthropic's Monday IPO filing and the $63 billion Broadcom chip-financing deal, which sent Broadcom up about 4%, plus record SK Hynix earnings overnight. Now comes a double test on Wednesday. The Federal Reserve decides on rates at 2 p.m. EDT and is expected to hold at 3.75-4.00% — futures markets put hold odds around 90% — after September's quarter-point hike, with officials signalling patience and some possibly dissenting in favour of a hike, since inflation pressure is now seen as demand-driven by the Iran-war energy shock, tariffs, AI demand and healthy consumer spending.

Then, after the close, Microsoft and Alphabet report, with Amazon following Thursday. The numbers behind the trade are enormous: combined backlog at Microsoft, Amazon and Alphabet is near $1.7 trillion against up to $600 billion of combined 2026 AI-infrastructure spending, with expected cloud growth of about 95% for Google Cloud, roughly 45-48% for Azure and 38% for AWS. Microsoft has forecast $175 billion in 2026 capital spending and on Monday offered voluntary buyouts to about 60,000 employees — more than a quarter of its workforce — to contain costs while funding AI.

What to watch: any dissent in the Fed vote Wednesday afternoon, then whether cloud growth can keep justifying the spending when Microsoft and Alphabet print Wednesday night — six days before the midterms decide control of Congress.

items.title: Rays rally for two runs in the 12th to beat the Brewers 4-3 and extend the World Series
items.summary:
Milwaukee was three outs from its first World Series title. Instead, Tampa Bay scored twice in the bottom of the 12th inning Tuesday night to beat the Brewers 4-3 at Tropicana Field, cut Milwaukee's series lead to 3-1, and force a Game 5. Rookie Cooper Pratt had led off the top of the 12th with a solo homer — capping a four-hit night — to put the Brewers up 3-2 and on the brink.

The rally started with an error: Junior Caminero reached on a throwing error by third baseman Joey Ortiz, and reliever Shane Drohan then allowed four straight singles without retiring a batter. Liam Hicks singled, Jonny DeLuca's single scored pinch runner Cedric Mullins to tie it 3-3, Chandler Simpson loaded the bases, and pinch hitter Ben Williamson delivered the walk-off single. Simpson had earlier driven in the game's first run and made a leaping catch at the wall in the ninth to keep it tied. Milwaukee's Jackson Chourio reached 10 hits in the first four games of a World Series — a feat previously achieved only by Babe Ruth in 1928.

One concern for Tampa Bay: Caminero limped off after going first-to-third in the 12th and was replaced by Mullins. Manager Kevin Cash said afterward, 'He'll play tomorrow with one leg' — his Game 5 status is the key watch item.

Game 5 is Wednesday night at 8:08 p.m. ET in St. Petersburg on FOX, with Jacob Misiorowski the likely Milwaukee starter. A Brewers win still ends the Series; a Rays win sends it back to Milwaukee for Game 6 on Friday.

items.title: Record king tides flood both coasts, closing roads in California, Florida and the Outer Banks
items.summary:
Record-breaking king tides flooded streets and low-lying neighborhoods on both U.S. coasts this week, with alerts running through Thursday and Friday in many places. The drivers lined up at once: the Oct. 26 full moon, warmer-than-normal water, a strong El Niño, a Kelvin wave pushing Pacific sea levels higher, and offshore storms.

In Los Angeles Harbor, the tide topped 8 feet on Oct. 26 — an all-time record for a gauge dating to 1923, with Tuesday's preliminary reading near 8.18 feet — and the National Weather Service warned of significant coastal flooding with tides up to 1.7 feet above normal, roads closed including sections of Pacific Coast Highway, and low-lying homes and businesses inundated. Miami set tidal records on four of five days, a streak a University of Miami researcher said could reach an unprecedented 10 days, with flooding in Fort Lauderdale and Miami Beach. Port Canaveral recorded its highest non-tropical water level since its gauge was installed in 1994.

On North Carolina's Outer Banks, sections of the coastal highway were destroyed; an emergency order barred visitors from Hatteras Island while crews rebuild dunes and roadbed near Pea Island. Florida's east coast sat under coastal flood warnings with gauges in the major flood range and 8-to-13-foot breaking waves.

Scientists say water levels like these preview what could become normal later this century as seas rise — and similar setups may recur at the new moon in two weeks and through the El Niño winter.

items.title: Teen arrested after a shooting near Florida A&M homecoming injured 12; prosecutor wins adult trial
items.summary:
Twelve people were injured — 11 shot, the youngest just 11 years old — when gunfire broke out shortly before 8 p.m. Saturday near Florida A&M's Bragg Memorial Stadium, just after the school's homecoming football game against Arkansas-Pine Bluff. Police say a physical confrontation between people who knew each other preceded the shooting, and they believe the injured bystanders were not the intended targets. Three people were seriously hurt and one was initially critical; no deaths were reported.

A 15-year-old suspect was arrested Sunday and faces 11 counts of attempted second-degree murder plus a firearm charge. At a Monday juvenile hearing, a judge ordered him held in secure detention, and Leon County's top prosecutor's request to try him as an adult was approved. Six of the victims were minors, including four Leon County school students and a FAMU student.

Among the wounded is Leon High sophomore and JV football player Tramon Jackson, 15, shot in the shoulder and back; his mother has started a fundraiser for medical travel and household costs. Another victim, 22-year-old Iyonti Smith, was transferred to a Gainesville hospital for surgery and faces at least another week there and three months in a neck brace.

The investigation remains open and police say more arrests could follow. Officials have also cautioned that viral social-media posts claiming missing witnesses or children after the shooting are unsupported.

items.title: Opioid deaths fall to their lowest level since the emergency was declared in 2017, HHS reports
items.source: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
items.summary:
Opioid-related deaths in the United States have fallen to their lowest level since the opioid public-health emergency was declared in 2017, according to a new analysis the Department of Health and Human Services released Tuesday in Detroit. The analysis, from HHS's Office of the Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation, was published alongside a Health Affairs Forefront article, and the CDC provisional data behind it show the overall U.S. age-adjusted death rate fell to 689.2 per 100,000 in 2025 — the lowest ever reported.

The pharmacy data underneath the trend, tracked from March 2015 to March 2026, move in consistent directions. Opioid prescriptions dispensed fell to 45.3% of the 2015 level, total opioid dosage dispensed dropped to 35.2%, and the number of patients receiving prescription opioids fell to about half. Meanwhile, patients filling prescriptions for buprenorphine or naltrexone — medications used to treat substance-use disorder — rose to 218% of the baseline, meaning treatment uptake has more than doubled.

HHS credits reduced unnecessary prescribing, fentanyl supply-chain disruption and expanded treatment and recovery, including the 2025 reauthorization of the SUPPORT Act and the DEA's Fentanyl Free America initiative. That framing is the administration's own; the verifiable core is the underlying trend — deaths, dispensing and dosage all down, treatment up.

What to watch: whether the decline holds when provisional CDC figures become final, and whether state-level fentanyl numbers follow the national curve.

items.title: Appeals court rejects the DOJ's bid to set aside 20,000 California ballots a week before the midterms
items.summary:
A panel of the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled 2-1 on Monday against the Trump administration's emergency bid to force Los Angeles County and California officials to set aside more than 20,000 ballots. The administration contends the ballots were cast by voters registered as noncitizens; on Oct. 13 the Justice Department sent officials a list of more than 20,000 names and demanded verification within 48 hours or segregation of the ballots.

The panel did not rule on the merits. It held it lacked jurisdiction because the DOJ appealed before the district court had adequate time to rule, noting the department gave the lower court roughly 15 hours — about three business hours — before seeking emergency intervention, and calling the claimed emergency 'at least in part… a self-constructed one.' The majority paired a Trump appointee with a Biden appointee; a second Trump appointee dissented.

California officials have questioned the list's accuracy: Santa Clara County found errors including three duplicates on the first page and said it would not comply without a subpoena or warrant, and an LA County sample of 200 names reportedly showed a high percentage were U.S.-born. Secretary of State Shirley Weber called the suit a reckless political stunt. The DOJ says 28 people on its list have been criminally charged with illegal voting, and the California case is part of a broader voter-roll campaign across about 30 states in which the department has lost 26 cases so far.

The underlying case returned to district court, where a ruling was expected Wednesday. For now, California's ballot-handling procedures stay in place for the Nov. 3 election, though the administration could still seek emergency review.

items.title: Residential world-cruise ship suspends its voyage in Cambodia over fuel costs, leaving about 200 passengers without their floating homes
items.summary:
The Odyssey, a U.S. residential cruise ship that set sail two years ago on a planned three-and-a-half-year voyage to all seven continents, has suspended operations in Cambodia — forcing the roughly 200 passengers who lived aboard to abandon what for many was their home. The ship, operated by Florida-based Villa Vie Residences, had a confirmed itinerary into November 2027.

The cause is fuel. Monthly fuel costs per cabin that historically averaged about $1,800 recently reached an estimated $6,000 to $8,000 in parts of Asia during the war in Iran. The company said it tried slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port but could not offset the surge: 'We have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses… Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution.' The ship docked at Sihanoukville on Oct. 23 for a planned five-day visit, was due to sail to Vietnam, and remained in port Wednesday.

Aboard were 203 passengers of 15 nationalities, mostly Americans, and 156 crew; the ship's capacity is 650 residents. Passengers were told to leave, with the company saying its focus is supporting residents and crew while it tries to restructure. Cabin buyers paid $120,000 to $440,000 to own, or about $3,500 a month to rent.

It is a direct, consumer-facing example of Iran-war fuel costs reaching Americans far from home — and a hard landing for people who sold or left housing on land to live at sea.

items.title: Brown and Husted deadlocked in Ohio's Senate race in the final days, new poll shows
items.summary:
A Suffolk University / USA TODAY Ohio Network poll released Wednesday shows Ohio's U.S. Senate race in a statistical deadlock less than a week before the Nov. 3 election: former Sen. Sherrod Brown, a Democrat, leads appointed Sen. Jon Husted, a Republican, 47% to 44%, inside the survey's margin of error of 4.4 points.

The undercard could decide it. Libertarian Bill Redpath and independent Greg Levy each polled 1.6%, and their combined roughly 3% is bigger than the gap between the leaders. Federal filings show a GOP-backed organization has spent more than $2.2 million boosting Levy, while a PAC linked to a Democratic nonprofit sent texts promoting Redpath over Husted — tactics Levy's campaign called 'highly undemocratic.' Brown leads big among independents, 52% to 24%, and Suffolk's David Paleologos said independents will determine the outcome.

Both parties are sending in their biggest names: Barack Obama headlined a Cleveland rally for Brown and gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton, and President Trump was scheduled to make his third Ohio trip on Wednesday. The winner serves the remaining two years of Vice President JD Vance's Senate term — and could tip control of the U.S. Senate.

The Senate race has recently shared the spotlight with the governor's race, where polling is equally tight. Final-weekend early turnout may tell the story before Tuesday does.

items.title: Ohio early voting enters its final stretch — and mailed ballots now must be RECEIVED by 7:30 p.m. on Nov. 3
items.summary:
Ohio's early-voting window is down to its final days. In-person early voting runs Wednesday through Friday, Oct. 28-30, from 7:30 a.m. to 7:30 p.m., then Saturday Oct. 31 from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., and Sunday Nov. 1 from 1 to 5 p.m. — the last day. Nearly a million Ohio ballots had already been returned as of Oct. 23. Cuyahoga County voters vote early at the Board of Elections in Cleveland, and photo ID is required in person.

The deadline that matters most has already passed, and a rule has changed. Absentee ballot applications were due by 8:30 p.m. Tuesday, Oct. 27. And under a new rule this cycle, a mailed absentee ballot must be RECEIVED by the board of elections by 7:30 p.m. on Election Day — a postmark alone is no longer enough. Officials advise allowing three to five days for mail, or hand-delivering the ballot or using the board's secure drop box instead at this point; only the voter may use the outdoor drop box for their own ballot.

On the Cuyahoga County ballot: U.S. Senate, Congress, governor, secretary of state, attorney general, auditor, treasurer, Ohio Supreme Court, state House and Senate, local judges, municipal and school issues, and statewide Issue 3, a proposed constitutional amendment. Election Day is Tuesday, Nov. 3, with polls open 6:30 a.m. to 7:30 p.m.; anyone in line by 7:30 p.m. can vote.

Polling in the governor's race is as tight as the Senate's — one survey has Vivek Ramaswamy up 47-45 over Amy Acton, another has Acton ahead — so the final early-vote weekend genuinely matters.

items.title: Cleveland schools will not renew Flock Safety — 201 license-plate cameras ordered suspended, $603,000 extension pulled
items.summary:
The Cleveland Metropolitan School District announced Monday evening it will not extend its contract with Flock Safety and has directed the company to suspend all 201 automated license-plate reader cameras on district property. The Board of Education had been expected to vote Tuesday on a one-year, $603,000 extension; the administration pre-empted the vote after what it called a broad review.

That review covered exterior security, site conditions and staffing, plus the privacy concerns raised by community and board members, law-enforcement input, and the cost of Flock versus alternatives. 'The District has decided not to pursue an extension of CMSD's contract with Flock Safety,' the district said. 'CMSD will continue its review of alternatives.' The original contract lapsed this summer, and Flock had kept the system running under a short-term extension. The 201 readers sit in parking lots at 62 schools.

The backdrop is an internal audit, presented Sept. 30, showing more than 500 outside law-enforcement agencies had access to the district's Flock data and searched it more than 130,000 times before outside access was revoked on July 6 — 92% of searches by non-local agencies. The district had previously told Signal Cleveland only CMSD security and Cleveland police could access the data; a spokesperson later said that was incorrect. Since July, only CMSD and Cleveland police have searched the system.

Without Flock, the district will rely on its nearly 5,000 district-owned cameras, Safe Passage workers and existing police and RTA partnerships; a district-owned, non-plate-reading camera alternative was estimated at about $346,500 up front. Akron separately moved to block nationwide searches of its own Flock network in the same news cycle.

items.title: Cleveland City Council refuses to reimburse the Browns $1.1 million for stadium repairs as the Brook Park move looms
items.summary:
Cleveland City Council on Monday voted down reimbursing the Browns for about $1.1 million in repairs at Huntington Bank Field, with the resolution failing 7-6. Council President Blaine Griffin voted with Mayor Justin Bibb's administration for reimbursement but could not find a majority.

The administration's position is that the work was necessary to operate the stadium safely and that the city is contractually required, under its lease for the city-owned stadium, to repay the team for such maintenance. The work was already done and deemed essential: a failed sanitary/sewer ejector pump, failed pipe insulation, cracked and deteriorated concrete, and overhead-door repairs among the projects.

Council members made no secret of the real issue: frustration over the team's impending move to Brook Park, after which the downtown stadium is expected to be demolished once the lease expires in 2028. 'People aren't happy,' Councilman Michael Polensek said after the vote. 'We're frustrated. We're not happy with losing the Browns, and we sure as hell are not happy with losing that stadium.' Polensek also blasted the deal in which the city accepted $100 million from the Haslam Sports Group in exchange for dropping its lawsuits over the move.

Because the lease appears to require reimbursement, the refusal raises the prospect that this fight ends up back in court — one more round between a city and a team that is already halfway out the door.

items.title: Ohio approves 10 expansion projects for 1,359 jobs and $2.2 billion — including 150 new Avtron jobs in Valley View and Seven Hills
items.summary:
The Ohio Tax Credit Authority approved tax-credit assistance on Monday for 10 projects statewide, expected to create 1,359 new jobs, retain 1,824 more, and draw more than $2.2 billion in investment and $142 million in new annual payroll. The projects were reviewed through JobsOhio and its regional partners.

The Northeast Ohio headliner is close to home: Avtron Power Solutions, a Legrand business unit that makes load banks — equipment used to test the reliability of backup generators and power systems for critical infrastructure — will create 150 new jobs and retain 285 positions in Valley View and Seven Hills in Cuyahoga County. The expansion scales up manufacturing, including 12 new product lines, to serve a growing customer base.

Avtron's VP and general manager Zac Bridgeman noted the company has called Northeast Ohio home since its founding in the 1950s, and JobsOhio CEO J.P. Nauseef called it a strong example of an Ohio manufacturer growing alongside fast-moving industries to meet rising power needs. The project was assembled with Valley View, Seven Hills, Cuyahoga County, the Ohio Department of Development, JobsOhio and Team NEO.

Elsewhere in the round: Spray Products Corp. adds 32 jobs in Medina, Rittal adds 182 in Urbana making data-center enclosures, Delaware Nation Investments adds 125 in Beavercreek in defense software and tech, Forgent Power Solutions adds 85 in Columbus's Arena District, and Bayer in New Albany was the largest single piece — 606 jobs by the end of 2034 under a 30-year credit.

items.title: Cleveland man pleads guilty to attempted kidnapping of a 2-year-old at Lakewood's Madison Park, sentenced to 5 to 7½ years
items.summary:
A Cleveland man pleaded guilty on Tuesday — the day his jury trial was set to begin — to attempted kidnapping and attempted abduction in the June attack on a toddler at Lakewood's Madison Park, and was sentenced to 5 to 7½ years in prison, according to the Cuyahoga County Prosecutor's Office.

Zechariah Crawford, 35, of Cleveland, admitted to one count of attempted kidnapping and one count of attempted abduction. The charges stem from the morning of June 19, 2026, shortly after 10 a.m., when Crawford allegedly grabbed a 2-year-old girl by the wrist at the park. A nanny at the scene fought back and got the child away; the girl was not injured.

Police used surveillance video and witness identification to locate Crawford, and he was arrested the same day. He had originally been charged with two counts of attempted kidnapping and one count of attempted abduction; the plea covered one count of each. The case was heard in Cuyahoga County Court of Common Pleas.

For Lakewood families, the plea closes a case that rattled parents all summer — a broad-daylight attempt at a neighborhood park that ended, prosecutors say, because a caregiver intervened.

baby.tip: Car-seat week: practice installing the Aria V2 base now, while there is no rush — click it onto the Vista frame once at home, check the level indicator, and route the seat belt or LATCH exactly as the manual shows. Then do one calm practice run of getting the base in and out of the MDX. If anything feels wobbly or unclear, a certified car-seat inspection station can double-check it — and your OB's office can point you to a local one.
baby.fact: Newborns arrive with remarkably good hearing: they have been listening for months in the womb, and studies show babies in their first days already prefer their mother's voice over a stranger's — and even recognize stories or songs heard often before birth.
baby.fun: Tiny prep mission for today: the going-home outfit draft. Each of you picks one newborn outfit (two sizes count as one pick — babies are surprise-sized), lay both next to the hospital bag, and let Moose sniff-approve the final roster.
